IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting الحسن بن أبي الحسن وثعلب: Most scholars, including al-Hasan and Thaʿlab, interpret amin as “O God, respond” or “Respond, Lord.” IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting الحسن والزجاج: A second explanation understands āmīn as “O God, answer,” held by al-Ḥasan and al-Zajjāj. BAYDAWI: Āmīn is an imperative-like expression meaning “answer” or “grant the prayer”; it is not part of the Qur'an, by consensus. BAYDAWI-FULL: Āmīn is an imperative noun meaning “answer/accept”; a report from Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet explained it as “do so.” It is built on fatḥa to avoid two adjacent still consonants. NASAFI: Amin is a spoken formula meaning ‘answer/respond,’ treated as a noun for the imperative just as ruwayd means ‘wait.’ It has long and short forms; the short vowel length is original, while the long form lengthens the hamza. NASAFI reporting ابن عباس عن رسول الله: Ibn Abbas asked the Messenger about amin’s meaning, and he answered, ‘Do it.’ SAMIN-DURR: Amin is not part of the Quran by consensus; it means respond and is an indeclinable imperative noun. IBNKATHIR: It is recommended to say amin after al-Fatiha, pronounced either with a long or short first vowel; it means “O God, answer.” A report from Waʾil says the Prophet lengthened it, and al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan. IBNKATHIR reporting أبو موسى: A Prophetic report in Muslim says that when the imam recites “nor the astray,” worshippers should say amin and God will answer them. IBNKATHIR reporting ابن عباس: A report through Juwaybir and al-Dahhak explains amin as “Lord, do”; al-Jawhari says “so let it be,” al-Tirmidhi says it means do not disappoint our hope, and most interpreters say “O God, answer us.” IBNKATHIR: The account of Moses' prayer and the dual reply that “your two prayers” were answered implies that Harun said amin; this makes the person who says amin to a prayer like one who prayed it. | mentions 10:88, 10:89 BIQAI: Amīn is a vocal form named for the imperative meaning respond. BIQAI-FULL reporting الحرالي: Amin means the petitioner trusts God not to reject the plea, since nothing can overcome or restrain Him; the word asks Him to respond. DURR reporting الحسن: Al-Ḥasan glosses Āmīn as “O God, answer.” DURR-FULL reporting الحسن: Ibn Shahin transmits Ubayy ibn Kab's variant with a repeated “ghayr” and amin; al-Hasan explains amin as “O God, respond.” ALUSI: Āmīn is an Arabic particle functioning as a verb, built on fatḥa to avoid meeting two quiescent letters; its correct meaning is respond, while another view gives it a broader sense including a synonym. BAGHAWI: Another view says Amin is God's seal upon His servants, protecting them from afflictions like a letter's seal protects its contents. NASAFI-FULL: The poet's evidence shows both long and short forms of Amin, and a Prophetic report says Gabriel taught Amin at the end of al-Fatiha, like a seal on a letter; it is not Qur'an because codices omit it. DURR reporting أبو هريرة: A weak report calls Āmīn the seal of the Lord of the worlds upon believers’ tongues. DURR-FULL reporting أبو زهير النميري: Abu Zuhayr recommends ending supplication with amin, like a seal on a page; the Prophet said a persistent supplicant had secured an answer when he sealed his prayer."}, {"id": "1:7/q27/p3", "position": "Āmīn means 'so be it'", "reasons": "BAGHAWI reporting ابن عباس وقتادة: Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada explain Amin as “so it is” or “so be it.” BAGHAWI-FULL reporting ابن عباس وقتادة: Ibn Abbas and Qatada gloss Amin as ‘so be it.’ IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting ابن الأنباري عن ابن عباس والحسن: One explanation makes āmīn mean “so be it,” as Ibn al-Anbārī relates from Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan. {"id": "1:7/q29", "question": "How is Āmīn pronounced?", "turns_on": "The cited reports, transmitted wording, and differing grammatical or legal inferences.", "positions": [{"id": "1:7/q29/p1", "position": "Short Āmīn", "reasons": "BAGHAWI: The reader should say Amin after finishing al-Fatiha, separated from it by a brief pause; it may be pronounced short or long. BAGHAWI-FULL: The reciter should say Amin after a separate pause; the word is normally light, though grammarians allow a long or short vowel, and means ‘God, hear and answer.’ KASHSHAF: Amin has long and short alif, both attested by poetry. KASHSHAF-FULL: Amin is an indeclinable sound used for the verb respond; it has long and short forms, and a poetic line illustrates it. IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting جبير بن الأضبط: Some Arabs shorten amin, as illustrated by Jubayr ibn al-Adbat's verse. IBNJAWZI-ZAD: The nūn is open in both pronunciations; āmīn has a short-vowel form amīn and a long-vowel form āmīn. BAYDAWI: The alif in āmīn may be lengthened or shortened; two poetic lines attest the forms, though their poets are unnamed. NASAFI: Amin is a spoken formula meaning ‘answer/respond,’ treated as a noun for the imperative just as ruwayd means ‘wait.’ It has long and short forms; the short vowel length is original, while the long form lengthens the hamza. NASAFI-FULL: The poet's evidence shows both long and short forms of Amin, and a Prophetic report says Gabriel taught Amin at the end of al-Fatiha, like a seal on a letter; it is not Qur'an because codices omit it. NASAFI-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Asked about Amin, Ibn Abbas reports that the Prophet explained it as “respond” or “so be it”; the word is a built verbal noun with long and short vowel forms. SAMIN-DURR: Amin has long and short forms, each attested in poetry.
